draft.title: Addition polymers
card: An addition polymer is made when many alkene monomers join into one long chain. Each monomer has a C=C double bond.
One bond of each double bond opens, and the carbon atoms link to the next monomers. The double bond becomes a single bond in the chain.
Nothing is lost in the reaction. The polymer has the same atoms as the monomers added together, so only one product forms.
Ethene gives polyethylene. Chloroethene (vinyl chloride, CH2=CHCl) gives PVC, with a chlorine atom on every second carbon along the chain.
draft.remember: Addition polymers form when C=C bonds open and monomers join, with no atoms lost.

a.q: What must a monomer have to form an addition polymer?
opts: A carbon to carbon double bond
A hydroxyl group at each end
A carbon to carbon triple bond only
a.why: Addition polymerisation works by opening the C=C double bond so that monomers can link in a chain. Two functional groups are not needed here, because no small molecule is given off.

b.q: Chloroethene, C2H3Cl, is polymerised to make PVC. A student has 1000 g of monomer. What mass of PVC can form, assuming complete reaction?
opts: 1000 g, because no atoms are lost
Less than 1000 g, because water is lost
Less than 1000 g, because HCl is lost
More than 1000 g, because bonds are added
b.why: In addition polymerisation the monomers simply join, so all atoms stay in the polymer and the mass is unchanged. Mass is not lost as a small molecule, which is the case only when a different type of polymerisation occurs.
b.clue: Count the products of the reaction.

a.best: A carbon to carbon double bond

b.best: 1000 g, because no atoms are lost
